name: Tapeworm diet

lead: The tapeworm diet is a long-running diet legend: a person deliberately swallows a tapeworm so it absorbs part of the food they eat, aiming for weight loss and a leaner look, then takes an anti-parasitic drug at the goal weight. Wikipedia lists it among 19th-century diet hoaxes.

The idea is that the worm competes with the host for nutrients. Medical sources describe taeniasis as often causing mild or no symptoms, with weight loss only an occasional sign of infection. No clinical studies have tested it as a weight-loss method.

paras: It circulates mainly as a story about extreme dieting rather than a routine with a defined method. In the legend, the worm is carried until the target weight is reached and then removed with medication.

Wikipedia notes gastric obstruction risk in the diet story. Cysticercosis from Taenia solium eggs can reach the brain, eyes and muscles and be serious or fatal, and the fish tapeworm can cause pernicious anemia by interfering with B12 absorption. Medical sources treat tapeworm infection as a disease requiring treatment.

social.title: The Horrifying Legacy of the Victorian Tapeworm Diet

angle.text: The story is that a swallowed tapeworm absorbs part of the food eaten, so fewer calories are taken in and the body and face slim down. It appears in accounts of 19th-century diet hoaxes, and medical sources describe the infection as a disease with serious risks.

lead: The tapeworm diet is a long-standing diet legend in which a person deliberately swallows a tapeworm, or its eggs, so that the parasite absorbs part of the food eaten and body weight falls. According to the usual account, an anti-parasitic medicine is taken afterwards to kill and expel the worm [1]. The goal is the one behind most weight-loss methods: a leaner body and face, which people associate with a sharper, more defined look.

Wikipedia lists the tapeworm diet among the 19th-century diet hoaxes in its article on fad diets, and notes the risk of gastric obstruction [1]. Historical retellings often tie it to the Victorian and Edwardian era's ideals of thinness, and popular accounts differ on whether the advertised pills actually contained live worms.

Medical sources describe tapeworm infection as a disease. Taeniasis, the intestinal infection with adult Taenia worms, is usually acquired from raw or undercooked beef or pork, often causes mild or no symptoms, and occasionally causes weight loss and loss of appetite [2][3]. If a person swallows Taenia solium eggs, the larvae can spread through the body and cause cysticercosis, which can be serious or fatal [2][3]. No clinical studies of deliberate tapeworm ingestion as a weight-loss method have been found.

paras: According to Wikipedia's article on fad diets, the tapeworm diet involves swallowing a tapeworm so that it absorbs food in the intestine; once the dieter has reached a goal, an anti-parasitic pill is taken to kill and expel the worm. The article groups it with other 19th-century diet hoaxes and mentions the risk of gastric obstruction [1].

Fad diets in general are described as non-standard, often short-term diets promising rapid weight loss, criticised by experts for lacking clinical research support and for risks that include malnutrition and regain of lost weight [1].

Retellings of the legend usually place it in the Victorian era, when slimness was fashionable, and describe pills advertised as containing tapeworm cysts. Several popular accounts also attach it to individual celebrities. Specific dates, products and people vary between accounts and are not documented here. A 2016 Hacker News submission titled "The Horrifying Legacy of the Victorian Tapeworm Diet" shows that the story circulates as a historical curiosity [4].

sections.h: What medical sources say about tapeworms
paras: Tapeworms have no mouth or digestive tract and absorb nutrients through their body surface; Wikipedia's tapeworm article lists occasional weight loss among symptoms of taeniasis [2]. The CDC describes taeniasis as caused by Taenia saginata (beef tapeworm), Taenia solium (pork tapeworm) or Taenia asiatica, acquired by eating raw or undercooked beef or pork, with most people having mild symptoms or none. Possible symptoms are abdominal pain, loss of appetite, weight loss and upset stomach, and passing segments in stool is the most visible sign [3].

T. solium infection can lead to cysticercosis, in which larvae reach the brain, eyes, muscles and nervous system; the CDC notes it can cause seizures, and Wikipedia describes eye involvement causing vision loss and spinal involvement causing pain or paralysis [2][3]. Wikipedia also describes the broad fish tapeworm, which can exceed 15 metres and can cause pernicious anemia because it absorbs vitamin B12 [2]. Diagnosis is by stool testing and praziquantel is the drug of choice, with niclosamide as an alternative [3].
No looksmaxxing forum material specific to the tapeworm diet was identified. It appears in discussions of extreme diets and fad-diet history.
